title: T-K-N
hook: tikkun, to fix, to set right

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-B-R: shever, a break, and mashber, the birthstool. Your line was breaking can birth. Did something crack, and did you ask what could start there? Today, the root that picks up the pieces. Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

"That which is crooked cannot be made straight." That's Ecclesiastes, Kohelet in Hebrew, sounding tired. The verb behind made straight is from today's root. He comes back to it: "who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked?" And yet near the end of the same book, the writer is remembered as someone who "set in order many proverbs," and the Hebrew uses the same verb again. A man who says crooked things can't be straightened spends his days straightening sentences. Today's root is the one he couldn't put down.
screen: `CROOKED CANNOT BE MADE STRAIGHT.` → `WHO CAN MAKE IT STRAIGHT?` → `HE SET PROVERBS IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: T-K-N. Tav, kuf, nun. Tikkun: fixing, setting right, putting in order. Turn it a few ways. First, the court. The Mishnah, in a chapter about divorce documents and freeing servants, keeps giving one reason for rules the rabbis put in place: mipnei tikkun ha-olam, for the setting-right of the world. It's practical. A rule so that a man can't quietly cancel a divorce document he has already sent, behind his wife's back, so that she believes she is free when she isn't. Tikkun olam begins as good order in a courtroom. Second, prayer. The Aleinu, said at the end of services, hopes for a day l'taken olam, to set the world right under the sovereignty of the Almighty. Here the fixing is God's, and it's on the horizon. Third, the mystics. The Kabbalah of Isaac Luria tells of vessels that couldn't hold the divine light and shattered, scattering sparks. The word for that shattering is shevirah, from yesterday's root. The work of gathering the sparks is tikkun. In this telling, the break comes first, and the fixing answers it. Fourth, today. Some Jews use the phrase for social action, mending the world through justice and care. Others hear the court or the prayer first. All of it lives in these letters. Kohelet may be right that some crooked things stay crooked. He still set his proverbs in order.
screen: `FOR THE SETTING-RIGHT OF THE WORLD.` · `THE ALEINU: TO SET THE WORLD RIGHT.` · `SHATTERED VESSELS, GATHERED SPARKS.` · `TODAY: MENDING THE WORLD.` · then, large: `FIX WHAT YOU CAN REACH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fix one thing. Settle, and breathe. Walk back through your day in your mind, and find one small thing left out of order. A reply you owe. A small mistake you noticed and let go. A drawer that won't close. A promise to call that slid to next week. Don't fix it yet. Hold it for a few breaths and decide exactly how you'll set it right. Then, when the bell ends, do it. If you pray, you can hold the Aleinu's hope in mind while you look. The bell holds the time.
screen: `FIND ONE THING OUT OF ORDER.` · `DECIDE HOW.` · `AFTER THE BELL, DO IT.`

segments.voice: T-K-N. Tav, kuf, nun: tikkun, setting right. And this week's lines in order: ask, answer humbly, free gift, vow, trust, breaking can birth, fix. Today's word.
Your line: fix. Today, set one crooked thing straight, the one in front of you, and leave the rest of the world for tomorrow. Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Tikkun appears in the Mishnah's court rules made 'for the setting-right of the world', in the Aleinu's hope to set the world right, and in Lurianic Kabbalah's gathering of scattered sparks; some Jews today use tikkun olam for social action.

fork.setup: you're a rabbi of the Mishnah. a man can quietly cancel a divorce document he has sent, behind his wife's back, so she may not know it no longer counts. what do you do?
options: leave it. the law is the law.
put a rule in place to stop it, for the setting-right of the world.
tell her to sort it out herself.
fork.reveal: the Mishnah says Rabban Gamliel the Elder ruled that it not be done, mipnei tikkun ha-olam: tikkun olam as good order in a court.

original.note: Hebrew: fixing, setting right, from tav, kuf, nun.

trapdoor: what you thought: tikkun olam is a modern word for activism.
what it means: tikkun is setting right: a court's good order, a prayer's hope, a mystic's repair.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Gittin 4:2's mipnei tikkun ha-olam, the Aleinu's l'taken olam, and Luria's shattered vessels.

notes: Ecclesiastes 1:15 litkon, 7:13 letaken, 12:9 tikken: all T-K-N. Confirm.

Mishnah Gittin 4:2 paraphrased: Rabban Gamliel the Elder ordained that a husband not convene a court elsewhere to annul a get he had sent, mipnei tikkun ha-olam. The chapter's other enactments (4:3–4:9) include rules on freeing slaves; the script says 'freeing servants'. Confirm the summary and the wording 'leaving her stuck'.
Aleinu: l'taken olam b'malchut Shaddai. Some prayer books read l'takken. Paraphrased. Confirm.
Lurianic shevirat ha-kelim and tikkun summarized in two sentences; no dates given. Confirm.
'Some Jews use the phrase for social action... Others hear the court or the prayer first' — deliberately unquantified. Confirm it reads fairly across movements.
